Overhead vs. profit — 2026, year to date

The year’s target is built in two columns: Column 1 holds the fixed items; Column 2 holds office salaries plus the per-head lines, figured from the roster — office and field counted separately — so the target recomputes the moment the roster changes. Phones count per foreman only. Crew wages are nowhere in it: they are job costs, not overhead. Overhead counts as recovered only when an invoice is paid in full. An invoice that was sent but never paid never recovered its overhead — that slice misses the mark by exactly that amount, and the profit inside it is lost with it. Half-paid counts as zero recovered. Visible to the Owner and the Operations Manager.

What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 92 — Call board (pilot)A new Call board (pilot) view sits in the left menu, right under Text delivery in the call-board area: the phone app's read-only window onto the same call-board records the web board above serves. It carries the board's today and this-week periods and the open items still waiting — missed calls with caller name, caller phone, started time, summary, text-back sent time, and waiting minutes, and waiting texts with participant name, participant phone, last message, and waiting minutes — in exactly the app's shape: a period plus open items. The view is read-only — no export and no intake on it. Viewing is Owner and Office Manager only; every other roster title is refused with the web board's denial message. Open Call board (pilot) in the left menu.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 91 — Estimate picking: lead offer + service catalogThe estimate detail on the Estimates view now carries a Pick services section above its Line items. From this lead offers the services checked on the estimate's lead — a Pick button per service, a Picked mark once picked, and a live count of services still needing pricing. From the service catalog picks any active catalog service, with or without a linked lead. A picked line starts at quantity 1, unit EA, $0 price and $0 cost, and the pick is audit-logged as a line added — “Picked line from catalog: <name>.” Picking an already-linked service reports already picked — never a duplicate — and a catalog pick of a service checked on the lead reads picked on the offer too, the same line. Picking is DRAFT-only and belongs to the estimating titles; the free-text Add a line stays for genuinely custom scope and is never treated as a pick. Open Estimates and scroll to Estimate detail — Pick services.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 90 — Geofence polygon editorThe new Geofences view (in the menu, under Field, next to GPS Tracking) is a visual polygon editor: pick a fence and it is drawn on the map as a polygon with its site pin marked. Reshape it in the vertex table — type a corner’s coordinates, delete a corner, or use Add vertex to place a new one — a fence never drops below 3 vertices. Save shape saves the redraw and confirms the fence in the same step; Confirm as-is confirms it without moving a single corner. A redraw that crosses itself is refused with the named error SELF_INTERSECTING_POLYGON, while a site pin outside its polygon only warns — it never blocks. Writing is Owner and Operations Manager only; every other title that can open the page views only. Open Geofences in the left menu.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 89 — Estimates final review (GATE 3)Every estimate detail now carries a Final review section — the last look before an estimate can be sent, sitting inside the send gate as GATE 3. Four items, each a reviewer's own attestation next to the system's computed evidence: deposit present, margin versus the 15% bar, terms loaded, and scope stated exactly. A partial save stays NOT_REVIEWED; all four attested makes it REVIEWED; and any header or line edit after that makes it STALE — a send after a change needs a fresh review. No review blocks sending, naming the missing review; STALE blocks naming the staleness — on the email send, the text send, and the gate display alike, because all three run the same gate. The approval gate and the nursery-quote gate are unchanged, and a review never bypasses either. Open Estimates and scroll to Final review — GATE 3.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 96 — Dispatch visits & the todos viewsOpen any job and a new Schedule — visits section books a visit: one-time or recurring, then a date, hours (required, above zero), a crew, and a service picked from the service catalog — there is no free-text service field, so a service outside the catalog cannot be booked, and an inactive catalog service is refused by name. The CBYD dispatch gate runs before anything is written: a digging service on a job with no 811 ticket on file saves nothing and says plainly what is missing. A saved visit lands on the dispatch board in its crew's lane and on the crew's My Day, moves an UNSCHEDULED job to SCHEDULED — never touching IN_PROGRESS, WAITING, or DONE — and feeds the job percent. Recurring visits form a series anchored on the first date, shown through the rolling 14-day look-ahead and capped by an end date when one is given; a series starting past the window still books its first visit. Visit visibility mirrors the money rules: office titles see all, Construction sees Construction only, Maintenance sees Maintenance plus Snow, and crew and CSR see no visits on this surface — crews still see their work on My Day. Todos now carry what they attach to — a customer, a job, or a person — plus a priority (Low, Normal, High, Urgent) and a progress (Pending, In Progress, Complete), with Done and progress kept in sync in both directions. My Todos, Tasks you assigned, and Assigned to Me are the three views over the same records, and the comment threads are unchanged. Overdue todos surface the same way overdue waits do: the Overdue todos list below — open, past due, oldest first, days overdue shown — and an Overdue todos section on the Daily Brief.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 77 — Change-order work areasOpen the David Gable drainage job (WO-SAMPLE-1041) — from the dispatch board, or from the Estimates view — and its change orders now sit in their own work areas. Every change order gets an area named “<reference> — <title>”: CO-001 — Added patio drainage is a fixed-price area with its own lines and its own $1,200 total, and CO-002 — Rock removal at the trench line works in a separate time-and-materials area. The sold estimate's lines (EST-SAMPLE-2209) show above them read-only — sold lines are never edited; added work goes in a change order, never into the sold lines. Each change order's detail carries its visible ID and issued date, its own Job Timesheet Tracking task linked to the job, the work area, and the change order, the purchase orders filed under its reference, and its hand time — with approved hours only in the count: time entered but not yet approved is shown and named, and does not count.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 74 — Revenue recognition, the cash distinction, and forecastingA new Revenue view in the left menu keeps two ideas apart that are easy to mix up: cash and revenue. Four cards lead it — cash received (every payment that actually came in), unearned cash (payments sitting on invoices not yet paid in full), revenue earned (only invoices paid in full count, at their full total), and outstanding receivables (what is still owed). Under them: revenue earned by month, an invoice table showing total, paid, owed, and earned side by side, and a jobs-underway forecast built from the dispatch board — jobs in progress or waiting, each with its proposed end date. The rules are strict: a partial payment is cash but earns zero revenue until the invoice is paid in full; a voided invoice appears in neither receivables nor the forecast; and a job with no budget figure reads Unknown — never $0.00.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 73 — Saved-data delete, the role matrix, and the sandboxTwo new views in the left menu. Saved Data shows the delete matrix — exactly which records each title may delete: the Owner, everything; the Office Manager, customers, leads, office docs, and tasks; the Construction and Maintenance Managers, their own division's jobs and estimates plus anything they created themselves; the Shop/Fleet Manager, equipment and shop tickets — no client data; and CSR, Foreman, and Apprentice, nothing. Two records sit outside the matrix: paid invoices and the audit log are never deleted by anyone, and the GM agent (Bill) never deletes at all — it only proposes a delete for a person to approve. Under the matrix, a delete form enforces it on sample records: pick a title, pick a record, and the matrix decides. Sandbox is the other new view — a live practice space, fully separate from real job data, with sample practice entries, a form to add your own, and delete open to anyone practicing.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 72 — Receipt lookupAny receipt in the system can now be found three ways. Open Receipts in the left menu and search by PO number, by memo text, or by customer — one mode, one search box. The samples prove all three: the masonry pickup receipt is found by PO-1040, an Other-bucket dump-charge line is found by its memo, and an off-site fuel receipt is found by its customer, Claris Design Build. Every result shows its PO, job, customer, amount, date, and memo, and Open brings up the receipt itself — its fields, its job, and a linked purchase order card that takes you to the PO. One sample receipt's total could not be read from its photo, so its amount reads Unknown — never zero, never guessed, the same rule cost tracking follows.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 71 — Maintenance contract estimate fields + hideA maintenance estimate now carries the contract itself. Open Estimates and find EST-SAMPLE-2207 · Center 111: it shows the contract start and end dates (Apr 1, 2026 – Mar 31, 2027), a monthly breakdown across all 12 months that adds up to the $31,200 contract total to the dollar, a per-service breakdown with labor, equipment, materials, and hours on every line, the total cost, and taxes as their own separate figure ($1,981.20). Every service line can be hidden from the customer, and so can the labor, equipment, materials, and hours detail. Hiding is customer-facing only — the sample starts with Irrigation checks already hidden: it stays in the record, its $2,400 stays in every total, and the “Preview what the customer sees” block shows only the visible lines, the hidden count, the total cost, the taxes line, and the monthly breakdown. Try hiding another line and watch the preview's totals not move.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 70 — Employee records: complaints, compliments, noticesThe new Employee Records view keeps every record about an employee in one place, in exactly three kinds — complaint, compliment, and notice — with a filter for each kind. A record is not on the employee's file when it is filed: it needs its approval legs first, and while approval is pending the record is hidden from the employee it is about. Once every leg is in, the record is recorded and the employee can see it. In this preview the list itself is empty: no complaint, compliment, or notice was carried in for any real employee — real HR records stay out of the demo. The approval-leg rules above are how records will work once they are filed in the live system. Open Employee Records in the left menu to see the empty list and the rules.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 69 — Day status + the iPad wall clock (CRM side)The new Day Status view shows one day at a glance: every person visible to your title, whether they are clocked in, clocked out, or not clocked, their open pairs, their closed pairs with hours, and hours so far — plus a day summary across the whole list. The punches come from two places that land in one record: the crew app, and the shop iPad wall clock, where a person taps their name to clock in or out. A wall-clock punch is sent shaped exactly like the punches the app itself stores, so both kinds pair up the same way. A punch that gets sent twice shows as a duplicate — it never opens a second pair and never doubles the hours. And a pair still open on a past date reads UNKNOWN for that day's hours — never zero, never guessed — until a manager closes it on the record. Open Day Status in the left menu to see the full sample day.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 68 — Customer cost trackingEvery job now carries its real cost in six buckets — materials, fuel, labor, equipment, subcontractor, and other — with change orders on their own line that never rolls into the job total. Customer money shows totals only: open jobs and finished jobs separate, split by season and year, never job-by-job, and never in the customer portal. Purchase orders count by when the money really moves — paid on the spot counts when paid; on account counts when picked up or delivered; credits and returns subtract as they land. Labor is hours × real per-person pay plus burden figured live at calculation time from the burden-rate records on file — pay and burden on separate lines inside the labor bucket, the total their sum, no rate or percent baked in and no fixed-percent fallback; until the office enters the records, burden and the labor total read UNKNOWN with the pay subtotal still shown. Trucks and equipment charge per hour, and miles never enter job cost. Anything that can't be computed reads UNKNOWN — never zero, never guessed. Open Cost Tracking in the left menu for the full picture, including the mowing fuel report. Verified: test-slice68 199/199, regressions green. Still open, not invented: what triggers a flag, the pay and hourly rates, meter automation, and the app sign-off wiring — plus the burden-rate records themselves, still the office's to enter.
What's new — Nov 2, 2026 · Slice 67 — Job status, percent & the Waiting viewEvery job now carries its status and percent per service, and the task-derived percent is always shown alongside the services-done count — the two numbers sit side by side, never merged into one. A wait is governed: putting a job on hold requires the service, the factor, who or what it's waiting on, and a check-back date — leave any one out and the wait is refused. Waiting jobs come off the dispatch board entirely. The new Waiting view lists every wait oldest first, with overdue badges on the ones past their check-back date and the full wait history on each. The Daily Brief gains an overdue-waits section, so a stale wait surfaces every morning. And the phone app gets its own pilot read: GET /api/pilot/waits, guarded by the same pilot-token sign-in as its sibling pilot endpoints.
What's new — Nov 2, 2026 · Slice 66 — Purchase-order section rulesPurchase orders now follow the section's approval rules, in writing. A division manager approves their own division's orders. An order that matches its estimate exactly stays with the division manager at any amount — no dollar cap on an exact match. A variance at or below $10,000 also stays with the division manager; a variance above $10,000 goes to upper management. In the field, a foreman approves a request on the spot, and the division manager reviews it after — the work never waits on paperwork. Overages are never silently absorbed: a material overage goes to a change order, a tool overage goes to overhead. Orders are numbered per job, with separate SHOP and HOUSE series for shop and house orders.
What's new — Nov 1, 2026 · Slice 65 — Staff list for the phone app's Team tabThe phone app's Team tab now has its own staff list from the CRM: GET /api/pilot/team, guarded by the same pilot-token sign-in as its sibling pilot endpoints. It returns a bare list with no wrapper — the app reads the raw list directly, so wrapping it would break it. Each row carries only 7 fields: id, name, title, titleCode, phone, crew, and division — no email, pay, rates, HR details, estimates, or invoices. The list comes from the CRM's real roster — User + Title + Crew — active people only, 10 active rows when it was built. Phone is empty on every row: the record has no phone column, so none was invented. There was no change to how records are stored and no migration, and no app changes in this slice itself — this slice is the CRM side only.
What's new — Nov 1, 2026 · Slice 64 — Fuel screens + the pump terminal connectionThe fuel records from Slice 60 now have their screens: open Fuel in the left menu for the fuel hub — the pump authorization screen, the four tank ledgers, reconciliation, and off-site purchases in one place. At the pump there is no fuel PIN and no fuel credential to enter: being signed in to the app is your identity. The camera checks your face — match and you can fuel; a different face is a hard deny; if the camera can't read a face, a manager approves it in the app. Try all three camera outcomes on the Fuel page. The pump reader itself talks to the CRM through a terminal connection that runs the exact same authorization rules — a face mismatch stays a hard deny at the terminal too, even with a manager approval attached.
What's new — Nov 1, 2026 · Slice 63 — Estimate remindersA sent estimate no longer just sits there. On day 3, day 7, and day 14 from the day it was sent, the customer gets a nudge — email plus text each time. The email nudges are sent; the text nudges are recorded as pending with nothing sent, the same honest pattern as the invoice ladder. Before every single nudge, the approval gate is re-checked — if the estimate's approval no longer stands, that nudge does not go. And won, lost, or draft estimates get nothing at all — no nudges, ever. See the per-estimate schedule on the Estimates page.
What's new — Nov 1, 2026 · Slice 62 — Invoice reminder ladderEvery open invoice now runs its own reminder ladder, separate from the Collections case ladder: email reminders on day 11, 30, 60, and 75. The day 20 text and the day 45 voice call are computed due and recorded as pending — nothing is sent on those two channels yet, and the record says so plainly. On day 30 a stop-service flag is recorded once on the invoice — it does not block dispatch and does not stop the reminders; it's a flag for people to see, not a switch. Paid, void, draft, and zero-balance invoices get nothing — no reminders, no flag. The ladder lives on the Invoices page, and inside each invoice's own record.
What's new — Nov 1, 2026 · Slice 61 — Invoice delivery & view trackingThe office can now see exactly what happened to an invoice after it left. Every delivery is recorded — the original send, every re-send, and every reminder — and every view is recorded with its channel (email link, customer portal). One timeline per invoice, newest first, with totals on top. The first view flips the invoice from Sent to Viewed; every later view is logged only — the status doesn't move again. All of it is internal-only: the customer never sees the tracking. Open any invoice on the Invoices page and its delivery & view timeline is inside.
What's new — Nov 1, 2026 · Slice 60 — Fuel records underneath everythingFuel now has a real record layer. Every fuel attempt gets its own fuel event — authorized, denied, or waiting on a manager — not just the ones that end in gallons. Each product keeps its own tank ledger — diesel, DEF, gasoline, and dyed diesel — deliveries in, dispensed out, expected vs. counted, reconciled; a shrinkage exception is raised the moment the difference is over 0.01 gallon. Off-site purchases link into the same records, tied to the truck and the job. There is no employee fuel PIN anywhere — the signed-in app session is the identity — and the camera rules are strict: a face mismatch is a hard deny, and a camera no-result needs a manager's approval in the app before any fuel moves. The screens for all of this arrived in Slice 64 — open Fuel.
What's new — Oct 30, 2026 · Slice 59 — Create invoice, and invoices on the dispatch boardThe Office quick-add on the dashboard is renamed: “Add a receivable” is now “Create invoice” — same widget, same place, new name everywhere it shows. And an invoice you create there no longer lives only in Collections: it now appears on the dispatch board under the Office crew. Open Dispatch, tap Office in the crew filter, and the invoice you just created is sitting in the Office lane — customer, what it’s for, and the amount — so the office’s own work shows on the same board as the field crews’. Try it: create an invoice from the dashboard widget above, then filter Dispatch to Office.
What's new — Oct 29, 2026 · Slice 58 — estimate lines from checked servicesOpen a lead in Lead Pipelines with services checked under “Services needing pricing” and a new step sits under Pipeline: “Estimate — lines from checked services.” Every checked service is offered as a pick — nothing is pre-filled and the estimate opens with zero lines; each pick becomes one pricing line (quantity 1 at $0 until you price it), picking the same service twice never duplicates its line, and services you skip stay listed as still needing pricing. CSR sees the picks and lines view-only; Shop/Fleet never sees estimate lines or estimate data. Try it on Mews Condo HOA (Maintenance board) or County Management Services (Construction board). Also in this preview: the SLICE 58 tag now sits in the top bar on every screen, and every title — Office Manager included — can change roles by tapping the role name in the top bar.
What's new — Oct 28, 2026 · Slice 57 — manager task progress trackerOne tracker now holds every task the Owner hands a manager, so assignments no longer live only in conversation. The Manager Task Progress panel sits right after the Slice 56 panels on every manager dashboard: the Owner sees all managers' tasks in one roll-up; each manager sees only their own. Every task shows its due date, its progress, and the date it last moved, with the full movement history one tap away — so whether the needle is moving is plain to see. A task past due and not done reads Overdue; a task with no movement in 7 days and not done reads Stalled — both are flagged in the panel and surfaced in the GM brief and the Daily Brief, feeding the accountability loop. The tracker carries no money fields anywhere, and creating a task stays Owner-only. The CSR, Foreman, and Apprentice dashboards are exactly unchanged — the tracker is manager-only.
What's new — Oct 27, 2026 · Slice 56 — manager dashboardsEvery manager title — Owner, Operations, Construction, Maintenance, Office, and Shop/Fleet — keeps its Slice 53 blocks first, exactly as they were, and then gains six new panels. My Tasks is the manager's own open work in one list — overdue first, then today, the next seven days, and later; todos and tasks with no date sit under “Needs a date,” because tasks carry no due date until someone sets one. Rollup shows one row per scope in view — open work, what sits unscheduled, what is over budget, what is overdue, the next milestone, and a health flag — counts and health only, never estimate or invoice money, so the Shop/Fleet visibility rule holds. Goals move on their own as linked work completes (jobs done, tasks done, shop tickets closed) — nobody types a percentage. Team Load shows each crew's and each person's open load for the week, so nobody gets loaded up while someone else sits empty. Status Updates carry the latest written update for each scope — progress, blockers, next steps — and a scope with no update in over a week reads stale. Inbox is the manager's own unread notifications, worked to zero: Archive clears an item, Follow-up turns it into a todo. Scoping follows the title: division managers see their own division (plus company goals), Shop/Fleet sees the company and shop scopes and still no client estimates, invoices, billing, or overhead, and the CSR, Foreman, and Apprentice dashboards are exactly unchanged — the six panels are manager-only.
What's new — Oct 26, 2026 · Slice 54 — real equipment names + the Inactive / Retired tabThe equipment module now carries the real names from MaintainX — 310 assets in 61 bundles, pulled Oct 26, 2026 read-only (MaintainX itself was never changed). The example gear is gone: the two made-up bundles — a 16-item “Mowing Box Truck” and a 3-item “Construction Trailer,” 19 items in all — were removed, and no sample equipment remains. The main equipment list on Shop & Fleet shows active gear only (304 assets); the 6 retired assets live behind the Inactive / Retired tab, one tap away — flagged, never dropped. Where MaintainX gives neither a description nor a serial number (50 assets), the field stays blank — nothing is invented. One scope note: bundle checks still count each bundle's full set, retired gear included — skipping retired gear in checks is a separate call, not bundled in here.
What's new — Oct 26, 2026 · Slice 53 — title-specific dashboardsEvery title's dashboard now leads with its own work. The Office Manager opens on “Office today — start here” — open missed calls, texts waiting, calls answered and missed today, the week's callback percentage, and open + overdue receivables — with the Calls today board first below it, then recurring tasks, quick-add lead and create invoice, dispatch across all divisions, billing, closeout, gate codes, today, and workload. The Owner leads with the Command Center and overhead; the Operations Manager with the Daily Brief and overhead; Construction and Maintenance each lead with their own division's jobs today; Shop/Fleet leads with non-productive miles, then shop notes and dumpsters; the Customer Service Rep leads with leads needing attention, oldest first; the Foreman with his crew today; and the Apprentice with his own day. Same one shell — title-driven widgets and order, no separate pages. Foreman and Apprentice see no company-wide figures and no other crew's work; Shop/Fleet sees no client estimates or invoices and no billing or overhead figures; and no title sees another title's private blocks. The company-wide Today figures do not render for the Foreman, the Apprentice, or the CSR — their lead panels replace them. The Updates feed is scoped the same way: the Apprentice and the CSR see only comments on their own todos and tasks, and a Foreman sees his own plus comments on tasks attached to jobs his crew holds.
What's new — Oct 26, 2026 · Slice 52 — the two-column overhead trackerThe overhead target is no longer one flat number. It is built in two columns: Column 1 holds the fixed items — all 12 amounts are still to be entered, so its total is carried from the $580,000 annual budget line until they are — and Column 2 holds office salaries plus the per-head lines figured from the roster (office and field counted separately: field $4,989.76/head, office $7,125.90/head), so the target recomputes the moment the roster changes. Phones count per foreman only, and crew wages are nowhere in overhead — they are job costs. The recovery rule is unchanged: overhead counts as recovered only on invoices paid in full, a partial payment recovers zero, and billed-but-unpaid sits on its own line. Ask Bill and the recovery projection now run against the two-column target, and every line whose real figure is still missing — comp rates, the SUTA rate, uniforms, benefits, per-seat software, phones, training, recruiting — sits on a still-needed list that names where the figure comes from. Nothing is invented or defaulted.
What's new — Oct 26, 2026 · Slice 51 — the General Manager agent is builtAgent #40 is Bill, the General Manager — now on the AI Agents roster (39 → 40), built and verified. The GM is distinct from Ask Bill (#39): Ask Bill answers from the SOP library; the GM acts and runs the system. It holds everyone accountable day to day — it surfaces what is overdue, names the owner and the date, chases it, and escalates to the Owner when it slips. From live records it builds the brief, the accountability list, and both weekly meeting agendas — each agenda 60 minutes, People's Wins first, with both sides in each meeting (a sales & admin slice in OPS, an operations slice in Sales & Admin), and the 24-hour email rule carried on the agenda as its send plan (the sending itself is not built yet). The GM's brief and agendas are Owner-only, and its switch is Owner-only too: switching the GM off pauses its briefs and agendas — the division agents keep working. It never approves its own recommendations — spending, bids, contracts, and pricing changes still need a person's approval.
What's new — Oct 23, 2026 · Slices 48, 49 & 50Three verified builds are in. Slice 48: Jake's non-productive miles panel on Shop & Fleet — every trip matched against the jobsite, vendor, customer, and shop polygons; trips that match none of them are costed per truck, and Jake can flip a call either way with the correction on record. Slice 49: the Overhead vs. profit panel (Owner and Operations Manager) — overhead counts as recovered only on invoices paid in full — plus Ask Bill's business reads: collections, pipeline, and overhead for the titles allowed to see them, problems answered in 1-3-1 shape, and a projection of the overhead recovery date that is always labeled a projection. Slice 50: geofences are property polygons everywhere — jobsites, vendors, customers, and the shop yard — never radius circles; the yard is its own polygon and matches as the shop itself.

Open Lead Pipelines: every lead card shows its fit score (like “🎯 92% — Strong fit”), the 🎯 Perfect Client button opens the profiles managers can edit, and tapping any lead opens its Perfect Client fit section, where answering questions builds the score criterion by criterion. Slice 15 is still here too: the Daily Job Closeout Check widget below, the 6 PM / 8 PM escalation ladder, and the crew's My Day banner.

Slices 27–37

Insurance & Subcontractor Compliance

Live

Company policy renewals, sub COIs + W9s, the baked-in subcontractor agreement — and a hard pay gate: no current COI or W9, no check.

Phone App & Equipment Tags

Live

The phone app is now the crew's daily tool, wired to the CRM. Everyone signs in by title — all roster titles — and sees only what their title allows. My Day shows today's job cards. The Job screen lets the crew check off tasks (each one needs a comment before it counts as done), add crew notes, and close out each day on multi-day jobs without closing the whole job. Clock in/out stamps the time together with the crew's location. Manager titles also get a Dispatch tab with the day's crews and jobs, and the owner's Snapshot — yesterday's numbers, today's crews, and approvals waiting — is visible to the Owner and the Operations Manager only. Customers are searchable right in the app, with the “Read This First” pinned-notes panel at the top of each client record. The equipment side from the pilot is still there: NFC tag registration and bundle checks, stored in the CRM, with all 20 real trucks from the GPS system loaded as bundles by their fleet labels — names like “T13 — 2022 Ford F-150”, each with its VIN. Registering tags stays limited to the Owner and the Shop/Fleet Manager; managers and the Foreman can run bundle checks. And if the CRM can't be reached, the app runs in demo mode on a built-in sample demo day with a visible “Demo data” badge — anything done offline queues up on the phone and sends when the connection comes back.

Recurring Jobs & Tasks

Live

Repeating work runs itself. Set up a recurring job schedule once — client, service, crew, budgeted hours, and the rhythm: weekly on picked days, every two weeks, monthly, or a season with start and end dates. The program then creates the real jobs ahead of time on the rolling two-week look-ahead, and each one is a normal job on dispatch, marked with a repeat badge. Any single visit can be skipped, and a whole series can be paused or ended — jobs already created are never touched. Office and team tasks repeat the same way: check one off and the next appears on its own with the next due date, assigned by title.

Issues & CI Board

Live

Anyone on the team can raise an issue. Each issue gets worked with the 3 Ws — who does what by when — and the 5 Whys, to find the real cause instead of just the symptom. Open issues automatically land on the Tuesday OPS meeting agenda, so nothing sits unreviewed. And once an issue is resolved, it can be turned into a draft SOP in the Help Desk with one click — so the fix becomes the standard way of doing it.

Post-Job Surveys

Live

When a job finishes, the client automatically gets a short survey on a simple link — three questions: a star rating, whether they would recommend us, and an optional comment — in English and Spanish. The score lands on the client record and shows on its history timeline. If the score is low — 3 stars or less, or a “would not recommend” — the Owner, the Operations Manager, and that division's manager are flagged the same day. One survey per job, one answer per client.

Lead Sources & Pipeline Report

Live

Every lead carries where it came from — Google, a referral, the website, a repeat client, a yard sign — picked from a list. The office enters what each source costs per month, and the report shows, source by source: the leads that came in, estimates sent, jobs won, the close rate, and the exact cost per lead. A weekly pipeline report generates itself on demand — new leads, estimates sent, won and lost with the dollars, and any lead that has gone quiet for two weeks, named.

Week & Month Close

Live

Week Close approves the whole week's crew time in one action — overtime flags itself, and once a week is closed its timesheets lock. Month Close is a checklist the program fills in itself: every pickup receipt matched, no finished job left unbilled, the maintenance payment schedules checked for billed-vs-earned differences, plus two office check-offs. When everything is clear, the Office Manager closes the month and that month's invoices and timesheets freeze — the only way back in is the Owner unlocking it with a reason, on the record.

13-Week Cash Forecast

Live

A 13-week look at cash, week by week. Money coming in: unpaid invoices and the maintenance payment schedules. Money going out: labor and weekly overhead. Every week shows a running balance, so cash is visible three months ahead. Any week that dips under the safety line is flagged red as a “Tight week” — weeks ahead of time, while there is still room to act. The owner sets the starting balance, the weekly overhead, and the safety line.

Owner's Daily Brief

Live

A brief at the top of the owner's home screen. It pulls together yesterday's invoices, payments, and finished jobs; today's crews and jobs; every approval waiting — estimates and invoices, with dollar totals; the scorecard numbers sitting red this week; and overdue meeting follow-ups. Only the Owner and the Operations Manager can see it — everyone else is locked out.

Meetings & Scorecards

Live

A weekly scorecard of 8 company numbers, each owned by a title — green when a number is on target, red when it is under. Some numbers are “lower is better,” like safety incidents, so red means it went the wrong way. The two weekly meetings run off it: the Weekly OPS Team Meeting (Tuesdays 9 AM, leadership) and the Sales & Admin Meeting (Thursdays 1 PM, leadership + advisor). Each agenda builds itself from the red numbers and the at-risk rocks, so the meeting starts with what needs attention. Since Slice 51, the General Manager agent (#40, Bill) builds both agendas from live records — 60 minutes each, People’s Wins first, both sides in each meeting. 90-day rocks show progress toward each goal. And every follow-up that comes out of a meeting — who does what by when — is tracked until it is done, with overdue ones flagged.

Rollup — open work by scope

One row per scope in your view, with a health flag, an owner, and a next milestone. Estimate reminders — Slice 63

For sent estimates only. Day counts run from the day the estimate was sent. Each nudge is email plus text: the email goes out; the text is recorded pending with nothing sent. And the approval gate is re-checked before every nudge — if the approval no longer stands, that nudge does not go.

The gate is re-checked every time

A nudge is not scheduled once and forgotten. Before the day 3, day 7, and day 14 nudges each go out, the estimate's approval gate is checked again. If the approval was pulled or the estimate's state changed, that nudge is held — the record shows it was checked, and why nothing went.

Who gets nothing

An estimate that is won, lost, or still a draft gets nothing — no email nudges and no pending text records. Drafts like EST-SAMPLE-2205 and EST-SAMPLE-2204 above never start the clock; the clock starts on the sent day, and only for a sent estimate still awaiting a decision.

Change orders on a sold estimate — Slice 77

EST-SAMPLE-2209 · David Gable — Drainage correction, the sold estimate behind job WO-SAMPLE-1041. Its lines are locked below, and each change order on the job works in its own area — the same detail the job record shows.

Slice 77
Slice 77 — Change-order work areasA sold estimate's lines are never edited — they stay read-only, exactly as sold. Work added afterward goes in a change order, and every change order gets its own work area, named “<reference> — <title>”, with its own lines and totals, apart from the original estimate's lines. A time-and-materials change order gets its own separate T&M work area, distinct from the fixed-price areas. Each change order's detail carries its visible ID and issued date, its own Job Timesheet Tracking task (job + work area + change order linked), the purchase orders filed under its reference, and its hand time — with approved hours only in the count. Names below are real Gold Coast records; dollar figures are sample figures.

Sold means locked

Once an estimate is sold, its lines are the record of what was agreed, and they stay read-only from then on. A correction, an addition, or an overage is written as a change order with its own work area — the sold lines are never quietly edited to match.

One change order, one work area

Every change order works in an area named “<reference> — <title>” — CO-001 — Added patio drainage. Its lines, totals, purchase orders, and hand time live in that area and nowhere else, so a change order can be billed, tracked, and closed without touching the original estimate or another change order.

Approved hours only

Hand time is attributed to the change order it was worked on, entered on that change order's own tracking task. Hours count toward the change order when they are approved — time that is entered but still waiting on approval is shown, named as unapproved, and left out of the count.

Estimate detail — Licenses & COI checklist

The estimator checklist on a draft estimate's detail. The items are picked from the Licenses & COI library — entered once there, never re-uploaded for this estimate. Checked items ride on the estimate when it is sent; unchecked items stay off it.

Slices 80 + 82
Slice 80 — Estimator checklist, DRAFT estimates onlyThe checklist exists only while an estimate is a DRAFT — once an estimate leaves draft, nothing more can be checked onto it. Checking a missing item is refused: there is nothing on file to send. Checking an expired item is allowed only after the estimator explicitly acknowledges it as expired, and the sent estimate carries it marked expired. Checking an item that is already on the estimate is refused — an item rides once, never twice. Unchecked items stay off the sent estimate; checked items ride on it. Checklist writes belong to the office titles — Owner, Operations Manager, Office Manager — plus the manager of the estimate's own division; every other title that can see the library reads the checklist without writing it, and crew and CSR get no access to it at all. Missing and expired are figured on read from the library, exactly as on the Licenses & COI page.
Slice 82 — Effective dates on this checklistEach row now shows the item's effective expiry date and its source — item, policy, or none — figured on read exactly as in the library: the item's own dates when set, otherwise its linked policy's coverage-line dates. Expired is read from that effective date, so the pollution liability COI — a sample COI with no dates of its own, linked to a policy whose line expired Jun 30, 2026 — reads expired here too and cannot be checked onto an estimate until you explicitly acknowledge it is expired. The crime / fidelity COI, also dateless, reads its linked policy's current dates (source: policy) and checks on normally.

Try the inland marine COI — refused, it is missing. Try the umbrella COI — it stops and asks you to acknowledge it is expired before it will check. Then open the same draft as the Construction Manager or Shop/Fleet Manager: the checklist is read-only for those titles. Open EST-SAMPLE-2207 and there is no checklist at all — it is approved, not a draft. Checks in this preview last until the page is refreshed — nothing is saved or sent.
Try Slice 82 hereOn EST-SAMPLE-2205, find the pollution liability COI: its row shows no dates of its own and an effective expiry of Jun 30, 2026 · source: policy. Check it — the checklist stops and asks you to acknowledge it is expired before it will go on, because the expired state comes from the linked policy's date. Acknowledge it and it rides on the estimate marked expired, same as the umbrella COI. Now check the crime / fidelity COI — also dateless, but its policy line is current, so it checks straight on.

Estimate detail — Final review

The final-look gate on an estimate's detail. Four attestations, each shown next to the evidence the system computes — the system shows the evidence, a reviewer makes the call. One current review row per estimate: NOT_REVIEWED, REVIEWED, or STALE.

Slice 89 · GATE 3
Slice 89 — Final review is GATE 3 inside the send gateThe send gate runs three gates in order: GATE 1 — approval (profit below 15% or total above $10,000 goes to the Owner / Operations Manager — unchanged), GATE 2 — nursery quote (unchanged), and GATE 3 — final review (this section). The email send, the text send, and the gate display below all run that same gate, so they can never disagree — and a completed review never bypasses GATE 1 or GATE 2. With no review on file, or a review still NOT_REVIEWED, sending is blocked and the block names the missing final review; with a STALE review, sending is blocked and the block names the staleness. The four items are reviewer attestations — the system computes the evidence beside each one and never checks an item itself. Reviewers are the Owner, Operations Manager, Office Manager, Construction Manager, and Maintenance Manager — crew, CSR, and Shop never review. Division scope applies: the office titles review any division, Construction reviews Construction only, and Maintenance reviews Maintenance plus Snow. The review section is DRAFT-only: a sent estimate shows the items as they were checked, with a stale banner when its review went stale.
Try the final reviewOpen EST-SAMPLE-2205 below as the Office Manager or the Maintenance Manager (its division's manager): check two items and tap Save review progress — it saves and stays NOT_REVIEWED, and both sends below stay blocked naming the missing review. Check all four and save — it turns REVIEWED with an audit note. Then tap Simulate a line edit — the review goes STALE with its own audit note, and the sends block again, this time naming the staleness, until a fresh review is saved. Try EST-SAMPLE-2208 as the Construction Manager: two items are already attested, but its sends still block at GATE 1 — the review never bypasses approval. Open EST-SAMPLE-2209 to see a sent estimate carrying its checked items and a stale banner. As the Construction Manager, the Maintenance drafts below are read-only — out of your division. Reviews in this preview last until the page is refreshed — nothing is saved or sent.

Estimate detail — Pick services

On the estimate detail, above the Line items: the lead's live offer and the service catalog. Picking a service adds its line to the Line items below — nothing is ever pre-filled.

Slice 91
Slice 91 — Picking is DRAFT-only, and only for pick-capable titlesA pick works only while the estimate is a DRAFT — a non-draft estimate reads “Picking is open on draft estimates only.” Picking belongs to the estimating titles — Owner, Operations Manager, Office Manager, Construction Manager, and Maintenance Manager; the CSR reads this panel without picking controls, and crew and Shop titles get nothing. The picker chooses from any ACTIVE catalog service, with or without a linked lead. An unknown service, an inactive service, or an empty pick is refused — inactive services sit disabled in the dropdown (in this sample catalog, Aeration is inactive). A picked line starts at quantity 1, unit EA, $0 price and $0 cost — the estimator prices it before send — and every pick is audit-logged as a line added: “Picked line from catalog: <name>.” Picking a service that is already linked to a line reports “already picked” and adds no duplicate line. A catalog pick of a service checked on the lead is that same line, so it reads picked on the offer too — and a later offer pick of it reports already picked. The free-text Add a line stays for genuinely custom scope: a hand-typed line is never treated as a pick.
Try pickingOpen EST-SAMPLE-2204 as the Office Manager: Mulch is already picked — it reads Picked on the lead offer and sits in the Line items at $0, marked Needs pricing. Pick Cleanup from the lead — a line lands at quantity 1, unit EA, $0 price and $0 cost, the still-needing-pricing count drops, and the audit gains “Picked line from catalog: Cleanup.” Now pick Mowing from the catalog — it flips to Picked on the offer too, the same line; pick it again from either side and it reports already picked, with no duplicate. Open EST-SAMPLE-2205 — no lead is linked to it, and the catalog still picks. Type Snow into Add a line instead of picking it: the line lands as a custom line, and Snow still reads not picked, because a hand-typed line is never a pick. Open EST-SAMPLE-2207 — approved, not a draft — and the panel reads “Picking is open on draft estimates only.” Switch to the CSR role (tap your title, top right) and the whole panel turns read-only. Billing sample — real customers, sample amountsCustomers below are real; invoices, statuses, dates, and dollar amounts are sample figures. No billing action is sent or saved.
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 75 — Invoice void requestsOpen any invoice below and its record now carries a Void requests section. A void is never one tap: the reason is written in, and someone else approves it — the Office Manager approves, unless the Office Manager is the one asking, in which case the Owner approves. Nobody approves their own request. How text delivery works

The rules behind this page, in plain words.

Slice 76

TEST provider — nothing reaches a real phone

Every send on this page goes to the TEST provider and stops there. It is a safe stand-in for a real text channel: the queue, the gates, and the log all behave for real, but no customer's phone is ever reached.

Unconfirmed — never a guessed result

The outcome column only ever says what the channel confirmed. The TEST channel confirms nothing, so every outcome reads Unconfirmed. The log never guesses Delivered and never guesses Failed — a made-up result would be worse than an honest unknown.

Gates are re-checked at drain time

A row can sit in the queue for days, and the facts can change while it waits. So nothing is trusted from when the row was queued: at drain time the system checks again — phone on file, the estimate's approval still standing, the invoice still open, and the collections case not paused. A row that fails stays in the queue, blocked, with its reason named.

No phone on file means blocked — never guessed

If the recipient has no cell phone on file, the delivery is blocked and the reason is written on the row: no cell phone on file. The system never borrows a number from another record, never tries the office line, and never guesses — the fix is a person adding the real number to the customer's record.

Try the drainTap Drain text queue (TEST) above. The four ready TEXT rows move into the delivery log at the top of this page, each with the outcome Unconfirmed. The Mews Condo HOA row blocks because its collections case is paused for a dispute, and the Betsy Kimmel row blocks because no cell phone is on file for her. Both VOICE rows stay pending, untouched. Changes in this preview last until the page is refreshed — nothing is saved and nothing is really sent.

How the pilot call board works
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 92

          

            
Same records as the web board
The pilot does not keep its own call list. It serves the same records the web Calls & Texts board serves — the today and this-week counts, and the open items still waiting. If a call or text is not on the web board, it is not here either; the board counts 3 texts waiting and names two of them, so the pilot names those same two and invents nothing for the third.

            
Read-only — no export, no intake
This view only reads. There is no export — no file, no download, nothing leaves the board from here — and no intake: no form adds a call, a text, or a callback here. Working an item happens on the web board and the phone system, exactly as before; this view is the app's window onto the result.

            
Owner and Office Manager only
Viewing the pilot call board belongs to the Owner and the Office Manager — the same two titles the web board's records are for. Every other roster title — Operations Manager, the division managers, Shop/Fleet, CSR, Foreman, and Apprentice — is refused with the web board's denial message, and no missed call or waiting text is shown to them.

            
Open items stay open until contact
A missed call or a waiting text stays on the open list until someone actually makes contact — dialing is not contact, and time passing never closes one. That is why the open items below the period counts do not change when the period changes: they are the still-waiting ones, carried with whichever period the app asks for.

Revenue
Cash and revenue are two different numbers. Cash is money that came in the door; revenue is only earned when an invoice is paid in full — and the forecast looks at the work still underway.
Slice 74

          
Slice 74 — Revenue recognition + cash distinction + forecastingThe four cards below are figured from the same invoice list on this page, so they always agree with it. Cash received counts every payment on a live invoice, partial payments included. Unearned cash is the part of that cash sitting on invoices not yet paid in full — money in hand that is not revenue yet. Revenue earned counts an invoice's full total, and only on the day it is paid in full — a partial payment earns zero revenue, however large it is. Outstanding receivables is what customers still owe on live invoices. A voided invoice is in none of it — not the cards, not receivables, not the forecast. How revenue works
The rules behind the numbers, in plain words.
Slice 74

          

            
💵 Cash is not revenue
A payment is cash the moment it lands. It becomes revenue only when its invoice is paid in full — and then the entire invoice total counts, not just the last payment. Until that day, every dollar paid toward it sits in unearned cash: real money, honestly labeled as not yet earned.

            
🧩 A partial payment earns zero
There is no halfway revenue. An invoice paid 90% earns $0.00; the same invoice paid 100% earns its full total. That keeps a big deposit from flattering a month it does not belong to — the revenue lands whole, in the month the invoice closes.

            
🚫 A voided invoice counts nowhere
Voiding an invoice removes it from receivables and from the forecast — the money was never really owed. The row stays visible on this page so the void is on the record, but it adds nothing to any card, total, or month.

            
🔭 The forecast reads the board
Forecast jobs are the dispatch board's own jobs — in progress or waiting — carrying the proposed end date the board shows for each. The budget figure is the job's own number from its record; a job whose record has no budget figure reads Unknown and stays out of the forecast total rather than dragging in a made-up $0.00.

          

          
Check the cards against the tableCash received ($18,525.00) minus unearned cash ($5,575.00) equals revenue earned ($12,950.00) — every paid-in-full dollar is earned, and every other paid dollar is unearned. Outstanding receivables ($13,815.00) is the still-owed column with the voided invoice left out.

        


        

          
Division budgets
Each year starts with one general budget for the whole company. The division budgets are split out of it — Construction, Maintenance, and Snow — and what is left after the split is the remainder.
Slice 78

          
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 78 — Division budgetsThe general budget for the year comes first, and the division rows split from it: Construction, Maintenance, and Snow — there are no Shop or Office budget rows. A division row whose amount has not been entered reads as unset, and while any division amount is unset the remainder reads UNKNOWN as a whole — the known split subtotal is shown, never a zero. When every amount is set, the split is reported exactly as entered, even if it goes negative — it is never forced to add up. A division row cannot be created until that year's general budget row stands. Only the Owner, the Operations Manager, and the Office Manager can write budgets; a division manager sees only their own division's row, and everyone else sees only whether a general budget stands — never company totals. All dollar figures on this page are sample figures.

          
Who sees whatLoading the budget view for your title…

          


          
How division budgets work
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 78

          

            
The general budget stands first
Every year has one general budget row for the whole company, and it comes before any division row. The division budgets are a split of that one number — they are not separate budgets added on top of it.

            
Three divisions — no Shop, no Office
The split has exactly three rows: Construction, Maintenance, and Snow. Shop and Office have no budget rows of their own — their costs live inside the general budget and the remainder, not in a division split.

            
Unset reads as unset — and the remainder reads UNKNOWN
A division row with no amount entered says so, plainly: it is unset, not zero. While any division amount is unset, the remainder after the split reads UNKNOWN as a whole — the page shows the known subtotal of the amounts entered so far, and it never shows the remainder as $0 and never guesses the missing piece.

            
The split is reported as-is — even negative
When every division amount is set, the remainder is the general budget minus the split, exactly as entered. If the divisions were given more than the general budget holds, the remainder is negative and shown negative — the system reports the split the way it stands and never forces the numbers to add up by trimming a division.

            
No general row, no division row
A division budget row cannot be created for a year whose general budget row does not stand. The general row has to be created first; only then can that year's Construction, Maintenance, and Snow rows be created under it.

            
Who can write, who can see
Budget writes belong to the Owner, the Operations Manager, and the Office Manager — nobody else gets a write control. A division manager sees only their own division's row. Every other title sees only whether a general budget stands for the year — never the amounts and never company totals.

          

          
Try itAs the Owner, Operations Manager, or Office Manager: the 2026 Snow row has not been created yet — create it, and the Maintenance amount is unset — enter one, and watch the remainder change from UNKNOWN to a real figure. The 2025 split runs over its general budget, so its remainder reads negative, exactly as entered. 2024 has no general budget, so its division rows cannot be created until a general row is created first. Changes in this preview last until the page is refreshed — nothing is saved.

When a cost counts — purchase order timing
A cost lands on the job when the money really moves, not when the order is typed.
Slice 68

          

            
Paid on the spot
Counts when it's paid. A card or cash purchase at the counter lands on the job that day, at the amount paid.

            
On account
Counts when it's picked up or delivered — not when the order is placed, and not when the vendor's bill arrives later.

            
Credits & returns
Subtract as they land. A returned pallet or a vendor credit comes off the job's materials the moment it happens — the bucket always shows what's actually in the job.

          


          
Fuel, labor & equipment — how each bucket is fed
Each bucket has one honest source. When the source can't tie a cost to one job, the cost falls where the rule says — it is never spread by guesswork.

          

            
⛽ Fuel — from the day's dispatch
Pump fuel is derived from the machine's dispatch that day: the machine was on that job, so its fuel is that job's fuel. When fuel can't be tied to one job, it falls to equipment cost instead — it never gets split across jobs by a guess.

            
👷 Labor — hours × pay, plus live burden
Labor is hours × each person's real pay rate, plus burden, on all clocked hours. Pay and burden sit on separate lines inside the labor bucket, and the labor total is their sum. Burden is figured live at calculation time from the burden-rate records on file — never a fixed percent, and no rate is baked in anywhere. A hand entry counts only when a manager approves it, and a flagged issue is signed off by the employee in their own app before the hours post.

            
🚛 Trucks & equipment — per hour
Trucks and equipment charge to the job at a per-hour rate for the hours they worked it. Miles never enter job cost — mileage stays a fleet number (see non-productive miles on Shop & Fleet), not a job number.

            
🧾 Legacy hand-typed cost
Old hand-typed cost figures don't vanish and don't get quietly re-based: each one stays visible as a manual adjustment line inside the Other bucket, labeled as what it is.

          


          
Labor burden — figured live from rate records
Burden is never a number typed in once. It is figured at the moment a job's cost is calculated, from the burden-rate records on file — each one a name, a rate, and the dates it covers — so when a rate changes, job costs move with it. The records below are sample samples; the real ones are the office's to enter.

🧮 Figured live, every time
Each calculation uses whichever records cover the work's dates. Change a rate and the job costs figured from it move with it — nothing is frozen at a number someone typed in once.

            
🚫 Nothing baked in
No rate and no percent sits in the code, and there is no fixed-percent fallback. If no record covers a date, the system does not reach for a default — it reads UNKNOWN.

            
❓ Until the office enters them: UNKNOWN
With no real records on file yet, burden reads UNKNOWN and the labor total reads UNKNOWN — while the pay subtotal still shows, so a job's pay cost is never hidden while the office catches up.

            
🔒 Owner & Office write the records
Only the Owner and the Office can add or end a burden-rate record. Ending one closes its window from that date forward — like the ended 2025 record above — and it never rewrites job costs already figured under it.

          


          
SHOP, HOUSE & office orders — where they land
Not every order belongs to a customer job. The destination is decided by the order's own series (Slice 66), and cost tracking follows it.

          

            
SHOP orders → the shop bucket
Shop orders cost into the shop bucket — the shop's own running cost, kept apart from every customer job.

            
HOUSE orders → excluded
House orders are excluded from customer costs entirely — they never touch a job, a bucket, or a customer total.

            
Office orders → the office bucket
Office orders land in their own office bucket, which is overhead — counted with overhead, never spread onto customer jobs.

          


          
Flags, quick invoices & deposits
The checks that keep the numbers honest.

          

            
🚩 Over-budget flag
Every job's running cost is held against its job budget, and compared with the won estimate's cost column. Cross the budget and the job carries the over-budget flag — like WO-SAMPLE-1041 above, $551 over — until someone deals with it on the record.

            
⚡ Quick-created invoices
An invoice quick-created from the dashboard counts toward billed right away — but its margin reads UNKNOWN, because no estimate stands behind it, and it requires a written explanation on the record. No explanation, no clean margin — ever.

            
💵 Every deposit links to its job
A deposit is never a loose payment: every deposit links to its job, so the money a customer paid up front sits against the exact work it belongs to — construction's 40/20/35/5 schedule included.

            
❓ UNKNOWN, never zero
If a cost or a margin can't be computed — a missing sign-off, a quick invoice with no estimate, fuel that can't be tied down — the field reads UNKNOWN. It never shows zero, and it is never filled in with a plausible-looking guess.

The shop iPad wall clock
How punches get from the shop wall into this page — the CRM side of the wall clock.
Slice 69

          

            
📱 Tap a name — that's the punch
The iPad on the shop wall shows the crew list. A person taps their name to clock in, and taps it again to clock out — no login, no PIN, nothing to type. The punch goes straight to the CRM.

            
🧩 Same shape as the app's own punches
The wall clock sends each punch shaped exactly like the punches the crew app itself stores — the same fields, the same form. So a wall-clock punch and a phone punch land in one record and pair up the same way, and this page never has to guess which kind it is reading.

            
👯 A re-sent punch is a duplicate, not double hours
If a punch is sent twice — a double tap, a retry after a hiccup — the second copy is kept on the record and marked Duplicate. It does not open a second pair, and the hours are never doubled. Crew B Foreman's 6:45 AM punch above shows exactly this.

            
❓ A past-date open pair reads UNKNOWN
If a day ends with a pair still open — clocked in, never out — that person's hours for that past date read UNKNOWN: never zero, never a guess at when they left. A manager closes the pair on the record, and only then do the hours become a number. Yesterday's open pair is in the day summary above.

How employee records work
The rules every record follows, whichever kind it is.
Slice 70

          

            
📋 Three kinds — and only three
Every record is a complaint, a compliment, or a notice. There is no fourth bucket and no free-form note type, so a person's file reads the same way every time: what went wrong, what went right, and what was put in writing.

            
✅ Approval legs before it counts
A filed record waits on its approval legs — the division manager leg and the office / HR leg, the same two-approval pattern HR actions use. The Owner can approve any leg. Until every leg is in, the record is pending and counts for nothing.

            
🔒 Hidden from its subject until approved
While a record is pending, the employee it is about cannot see it at all — it does not appear in their file, not even as a placeholder. The moment the last leg lands, the record is recorded and visible to that employee, once it is recorded.

            
🗂️ Records stay on file
A recorded record is never deleted. If something about it changes, the change is a new entry in the record's history — who did what, and when — so the file always shows the full story, not just the latest version.

Approvals in this preview last until the page is refreshed — nothing is saved.

How receipt lookup works
Where receipts come from, and how each one ties back to a job and a cost.

🔎 Three ways in — one field each
The mode decides what the box searches: the PO number on the receipt, the words in its memo, or the customer the receipt belongs to. Nothing else is searched, so a hit always tells you exactly why it matched.

            
🧾 Every receipt lands on a job
However a receipt arrives — a pickup photo, an off-site fuel purchase, or a hand entry from a gate ticket — it carries its job and its cost bucket (materials, fuel, labor, equipment, subcontractor, or other), so its cost lands in the same buckets Cost Tracking reads.

            
🔗 The linked PO is one tap away
When a purchase order stands behind the receipt, the detail shows a linked-PO card — the PO number, its vendor, and its status — with a link straight to that purchase order. A purchase made with no PO opened says so on the card instead of inventing one.

            
❓ An unresolvable amount reads Unknown
If a receipt's total cannot be read or resolved — a blurred photo, a torn ticket — the amount reads Unknown. It is never shown as zero and never filled in with a plausible number; the office resolves it on the record, and until then the job's cost says the same.

How delete works
The rules behind the matrix, in plain words.
Slice 73

          

            
🗂️ The matrix decides, not the person
Delete rights come from the title, never from who asks loudest. A title either holds the row in the matrix or it does not — and the same check runs every time, on every record, so there is no side door around it.

            
✍️ Your own work is yours to remove
The Construction and Maintenance Managers hold one extra right: anything they created themselves, even outside their own job and estimate rows. It is how a manager cleans up their own mistake without waiting on the office — and it stops at records someone else created.

            
🤖 The GM agent only proposes
Bill, the GM agent, never deletes anything. When a record looks like it should go, the agent files a delete proposal — the record, the reason, and who it waits on — and a person holding the matrix row makes the call. Try it in the form above: pick GM agent (Bill) and any record.

            
🔒 Two records are never deleted
A paid invoice is money already collected — it stays, so the books always tie out. The audit log is the record of every change, deletes included — if it could be deleted, nothing else in it could be trusted. Both rows read Never for every title, the Owner included.

          

          
Try the edges of the matrixAs Foreman, try to delete the customer — denied: crew titles hold no delete rights. As GM agent (Bill), try anything: nothing deletes, a proposal is filed instead. And as Owner, try the paid invoice: even the top of the matrix stops there.

How the sandbox works
Why practice data gets its own space — and its own delete rule.
Slice 73

          

            
🧪 Separate on purpose
Sandbox entries are stored apart from real records. They cannot be dispatched, invoiced, or sent to a customer, and they never show up in search results for real work — the wall between practice and real is the whole point.

            
🙌 Delete is open here
On real records, delete follows the role matrix in Saved Data. In the sandbox, anyone practicing may delete any entry — cleaning up after your own practice, or someone else's, is part of learning, and nothing real can be lost.

            
🎓 Built for learning the buttons
New hires and anyone rehearsing a flow work here first: build a fake job, price a fake estimate, delete it, build it again. When the same steps feel easy here, they are safe to do on the real views.

            
🏷️ Practice is labeled practice
Every sandbox entry carries its Practice kind and the name of the person practicing, so a practice entry can never be mistaken for real work — and real work never wears a practice label.

Ask Bill — in plain English

              
Ask Bill (agent #39) belongs to every role. It answers how-to questions only from the company’s approved SOP / how-to library — the written Gold Coast way, never an invented way. If the library doesn’t cover a question, it says so and routes the question to the Help Desk queue. New in Slice 49, it also reads the business — collections, the pipeline, and overhead — for the titles allowed to see those numbers, answers problems in 1-3-1 shape (one problem, three options, one recommendation), and may project the date overhead recovery completes, always labeled a projection. It guides and explains; it doesn’t do the work, change records, or touch approvals, money, or sends. Not the General Manager — that is agent #40, Bill, in the spotlight below.

              

                
                
              

              

            

            

              
🛡️ Guardrails — built in, not optional

              
    
                
  • Spending, bids, contracts, and pricing changes need human approval — an agent prepares, a person decides.
    • 
                
  • Estimates over the gate (profit under 15% or total over $10,000) wait for upper-management approval before they can be sent.
    • 
                
  • Invoices over the same gate wait for approval before they can be sent, and the person who requested approval can’t approve their own.
    • 
                
  • An agent that is switched off takes no actions at all — no drafts, no sends, no calls — until the Owner switches it back on.
    • 
                
  • The General Manager (#40) never approves its own recommendations — it surfaces, names, dates, chases, and escalates; a person decides. Switching the GM off pauses only its briefs and agendas — the division agents keep working.
    • 
                
  • Agents follow the 1-3-1 rule: one problem stated plainly, three real options, one recommendation. The person always decides.
    • 
              

            

          

          

              
⭐ General Manager — Bill (agent #40) · New in Slice 51

              
THE GM ACTS — while Ask Bill (#39) ANSWERS. Ask Bill explains from the SOP library and changes nothing; the General Manager runs the system day to day.

              
The GM oversees and coordinates the other 39 agents and holds everyone accountable day to day — all titles, all divisions — covering the accountability function of the open Operations Manager seat. Its loop never changes: surface what is overdue or at risk, name the owner and the date, chase it until it moves, and escalate to the Owner when it slips. Open commitments stay visible until they are closed — nothing is carried from memory.

              
From live records the GM builds the owner's brief, the accountability list, and both weekly meeting agendas — and chairs the Tuesday OPS meeting as the accountability review and runs Thursday's Sales & Admin meeting from its agenda. Each agenda is built the day before, timeboxed to exactly 60 minutes, opens with People's Wins, carries both sides (operations plus a sales & admin slice on Tuesday; pipeline and admin plus an operations slice on Thursday), and carries the 24-hour email rule as its send plan: OPS to the leadership team Monday 9 AM, Sales & Admin to leadership + advisor Wednesday 1 PM. What does not fit stays on the agenda as a carried-forward commitment. The brief and the agendas are Owner-only. The GM prepares and escalates — it never approves its own recommendations.

How credit-application drafts work
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 79

          

            
Filled from the company profile — six categories only
Auto-fill draws on the company profile and nothing else, and only in these categories: legal name, addresses, phones, registrations, tax identifiers, bank references, and trade references. Anything outside those categories is never pulled in.

            
Blank stays blank — “Still needed”
When the profile holds no value for a field, the field is left blank and marked Still needed. The system never guesses a value, never copies a similar one in, and never shows a made-up number as if it were on file.

            
Bank references: name and contact only
A bank reference fills the bank's name and its contact — nothing more. A bank account number is never filled and never stored, and neither is a credit card number. Those lines are not part of any draft on this page.

            
Owner-only rows — never on the profile
The Owner's Social Security number, date of birth, and personal guarantee are personal. They are never stored on the company profile and never auto-filled. The rows stay visible on the form, marked Owner only, and only the Owner can type into them.

            
A draft is not a submission
Nothing here is submitted and nothing is signed. The draft exists so a person can review and correct every line before anything is sent anywhere — sending happens outside this page, by a person, after review.

            
Approval is per form — and corrections clear it
Approving one application never carries over to another — each form is approved on its own. If an approved form is corrected afterward, it goes back to DRAFT and the approval is cleared, so it has to be reviewed and approved again. Approving a form that is already approved, with no changes, is refused.

            
Office titles only
This view is open to the Owner, the Operations Manager, and the Office Manager — and to no other title. Credit applications carry the company's registrations and tax identifiers, so they stay with the office titles.

Then open the Sample Contractor Supply draft: it is still a plain DRAFT, because approval never carries over. Changes in this preview last until the page is refreshed — nothing is saved, submitted, or signed.

How the library works
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 80

          

            
Entered once — never re-uploaded
A license or COI is entered in this library one time. An estimate that needs it picks it from the library on the estimator checklist (on the Estimates page) — nobody uploads the same certificate again for the next job or the next estimate, and there is only ever one copy to renew.

            
On file — or missing
An item counts as on file when any one of these is present: a file reference, details, or a linked insurance policy. An item with none of the three is missing — like the inland marine COI above, which has been asked for and not yet received. Missing is figured fresh on every read, so the moment any one of the three lands on the record, the item is on file.

            
Expired — figured from the date
An item is expired when its expiration date is before today — figured on read, so an item flips to expired on its own the morning after it runs out, with nobody editing the record. An item with no expiration date — like the shop's local license above — is never expired, no matter how much time passes.

            
Who can see the library
The Owner, the Operations Manager, the Office Manager, and the Construction, Maintenance, and Shop/Fleet managers can open this view. Crew titles and the Customer Service Representative get no access — the menu entry is hidden for them, and the library itself is not shown to them here either.

          

          
Per-line insurance dates — how the effective dates are read
The Slice 82 rules behind the dates on the cards above.
Slice 82

          

            
Effective dates — own dates win
For a COI linked to an insurance policy, the effective dates are the item's own effective and expiration dates when they are set. Only when the item carries no dates of its own are the dates read from the linked policy's coverage line. Own dates always win — a policy's dates never override dates recorded on the item itself.

            
Expired reads the effective date
An item is expired when its effective expiration date — whichever source supplied it — is before today. That is why the dateless pollution liability COI above reads expired: its linked policy's coverage line expired Jun 30, 2026. On the estimator checklist it is treated exactly like any other expired item — it can only be checked on after the explicit expired acknowledgment. An item with no effective expiration date from either source is never expired.

            
The source is always named
Every card and every checklist row shows the effective expiry date plus its source: item when the item's own dates are used, policy when the linked policy's coverage-line dates are used, or none when neither the item nor a linked policy carries dates — like the shop license.

            
Computed on read — renewals flow at once
Effective dates are figured fresh on every read from the item and its linked policy — they are never copied onto the item as stored dates. When a policy is renewed and its coverage-line dates move, every dateless item linked to that policy shows the new dates immediately, with nobody editing the items.
