How asset sales work
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 81

          

            
Both copies, on the asset's record
When an asset is sold, two copies of the bill of sale are filed on that asset's record — not in a shared folder, not on the buyer's record. Anyone opening the asset sees the sale and its paperwork together, and both copies stay attached after the asset is retired-sold.

            
The blank form is stored once
The blank bill-of-sale form lives in one central place and is reused for every sale. Nobody uploads a fresh blank for each asset, and the blank itself is never filled in — each sale produces its own filled copy from it.

            
Sale facts are entered by hand
The equipment item, buyer, asset identification, price, date, filled-copy reference, and signatures note are typed in by hand for each sale. They are never derived from the equipment item row — what the catalog row says about the asset does not fill in what the sale record says about the sale.

            
Price is stored in whole cents
A sale price is kept as a whole number of cents — $1,275.50 is stored as 127550 — so a price never drifts by rounding. The record shows the dollar figure and the cents it is stored as, side by side.

            
Missing paperwork is figured on read
A sale whose record has no filled-copy file reference reads as missing paperwork. That is computed every time the record is read, never stored as a flag — the moment the filled copy is filed on the sale, the flag is gone, with nobody editing a status.

            
Retired, never deleted
A sold asset is retired-sold, never deleted: the record, its sales, and both copies of the bill of sale stay on file. An asset with sales cannot be deleted at all, and retiring an asset that is already retired-sold is refused — it was already done, once.

            
Who sees it, who writes it
The Owner, the Operations Manager, the Office Manager, the Construction and Maintenance managers, and the Shop/Fleet Manager can open this view. Writes — recording a sale, filing a filled copy, retire-sold — belong to the office titles plus the Shop/Fleet Manager; division managers read only. Crew titles and the CSR get no access.

Read the Billy Goat blower record: its filled copy was never filed, so it reads MISSING PAPERWORK — file the copy from that sale (office titles and Shop/Fleet only) and the flag clears on the spot, because it is figured on read. Then switch titles at the top: a division manager reads everything but every write is refused, and the CSR and crew titles get no access at all. Equipment financing
One financing record per financed asset — lender, terms, a computed amortization schedule, a payment tracker, write-offs, and the January interest-letter routine.
Slice 93

          
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 93 — Equipment financingEach record carries one financed asset: lender, original amount, rate, term, start date, payment amount, and payment day. The amortization schedule is computed from those terms — due date, payment, principal part, interest part, and remaining balance are never typed by hand. Monthly rate is the annual rate ÷ 12, interest is rounded to whole cents, principal is the rest, and the final payment is trimmed so the balance lands exactly on zero. Marking a payment applies interest first, the rest to principal: the full scheduled remainder is PAID, anything less is PARTIAL, and MISSED is marked by a person only — never automatic. Remaining balance is the original minus principal actually applied minus approved write-offs; next due is the earliest payment still owed, flagged when overdue. A marking that zeroes the balance closes the schedule as PAID_OFF and turns every still-open row CLOSED; a write-off that zeroes it closes as WRITTEN_OFF. A second financing record for the same asset is refused, and terms that cannot pay the loan off are refused with a named error. Interest-letter figures come from payment markings, never scheduled figures, and each letter is generated once per year plus lender. Assets, lenders, and every dollar figure on this page are samples for this preview. Viewing is the office titles, the division managers, and the Shop/Fleet Manager; writes are the office titles plus the Shop/Fleet Manager; write-off approval is the Owner or the Office Manager only. Crew and CSR get no access.

          
Who sees whatLoading the financing records for your title…

          


          
How equipment financing works
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 93

          

            
One record per financed asset
Each financing record belongs to exactly one asset and carries the lender, original amount, rate, term, start date, payment amount, and payment day. An asset that already has a record cannot get a second one — the create is refused.

            
The schedule is computed, never typed
Due dates fall on the payment day each month from the start date. Interest for a month is the balance times the annual rate ÷ 12, rounded to whole cents; principal is the payment minus that interest; the last payment is trimmed so the balance lands on exactly zero.

            
Terms that can't pay off are refused
If the payment does not cover the first month's interest, the record is refused with PAYMENT_DOES_NOT_COVER_FIRST_INTEREST. If the term ends with a balance still remaining, it is refused with TERM_ENDS_WITH_BALANCE_REMAINING. Nothing half-valid is saved.

            
Marking applies interest first
Every amount marked on a scheduled payment pays that payment's interest first, and the rest goes to principal. Paying the full scheduled remainder marks the row PAID; less marks it PARTIAL and it stays the next due. MISSED is a person's call only — the system never marks a payment missed on its own.

            
Balance and next due are always live
Remaining balance = original amount − principal actually applied − approved write-offs. Next due is the earliest payment still owed — scheduled, partial, or marked missed — with an overdue flag once its date has passed. Total interest paid counts only interest from actual markings.

            
Closing: PAID_OFF or WRITTEN_OFF
When a marking brings the balance to zero, the schedule closes as PAID_OFF and every still-open row turns CLOSED. When an approved write-off brings it to zero, it closes as WRITTEN_OFF instead. Closed schedules take no more markings.

            
Write-offs need a reason and approval
A remaining balance can be written off only with a reason and approval from the Owner or the Office Manager — nobody else can approve one. The year-end write-off summary lists every write-off, and each amount is added to that equipment's total cost.

            
January interest letters
Each January, a reminder goes to the Office Manager to request an interest-paid letter from each equipment lender for the prior year. The figures come from payment markings — never the scheduled figures — and each letter is generated once per year plus lender (idempotent), moving PENDING → REQUESTED → RECEIVED.

            
Who can do what
View: office titles (Owner, Operations Manager, Office Manager), the division managers, and the Shop/Fleet Manager. Write (create records, mark payments, move letters): office titles plus the Shop/Fleet Manager — division managers read only. Approve a write-off: Owner or Office Manager only. Crew and CSR: no access at all.

          

        


        

          
Vendor portals
Every asset linked to the vendor website where its invoices live — dealer, manufacturer, or supplier portal. The link carries the login step; the login itself stays in the password vault.
Slice 94

          
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 94 — CMMS vendor portal linksWhen an asset is added, its record carries the login step for the vendor website where that asset's invoices live — a dealer, manufacturer, or supplier portal. The login itself is stored in the CRM password vault — it is never typed into the asset record in plain text, and no credential, password, key, or secret field exists anywhere in this view. The login step is required, but an asset with no vendor site is marked “none” instead of blocking the add. One link per asset — a second link for the same asset is refused — and every link starts PENDING_SETUP and stays unverified until a live check confirms it. Once linked, the CRM pulls that asset's invoices from the website into the asset record, so purchase, parts, and service invoices land on the asset without hand entry. In this preview there is no live integration, so every pull honestly records NOT_CONNECTED with its reason named — no portal address is named first, then no vault login, then no live integration. Unlinking is refused while invoices or pull attempts ride on the link. Invoices recorded by hand are MANUAL_ENTRY only; PORTAL_SYNC is reserved for the future live pull and is never used by hand. An invoice amount of null means not on file — never zero — and a duplicate portal invoice number on the same link is refused. No specific vendor connection is named — the rule is the behavior, for any vendor site. Assets and vendors below are samples; every dollar figure is a sample. Viewing is the office titles, the division managers, and the Shop/Fleet Manager; writes are the office titles plus the Shop/Fleet Manager. Crew and CSR get no access.

          
Who sees whatLoading the vendor portal links for your title…

          


          
How vendor portal links work
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 94

          

            
The login step lives on the asset record
When an asset is added, its record includes the login step for the vendor website where that asset's invoices live — the dealer, manufacturer, or supplier portal for that asset. The step says where to go and what to open. It is not the login itself.

            
The login itself stays in the vault
The actual sign-in is stored in the CRM password vault — never typed into the asset record in plain text. This view holds no credential, password, key, or secret anywhere: there is no column and no field for one, and nothing on this page ever asks for one.

            
Required — or marked “none”
The login step is required on every link. An asset that has no vendor site does not block the add: its login step is marked “none”, its vendor reads as no vendor site, and it carries no portal address. Anything else with a blank step is refused.

            
One link per asset, starting PENDING_SETUP
An asset carries one vendor portal link — a second link for the same asset is refused. Every new link starts at PENDING_SETUP and unverified; no one can type a link into a verified or set-up state. Only a future live check can verify one.

            
Linked means invoices land on the asset
Once an asset is linked, the CRM pulls that asset's invoices from the vendor website into the asset record — purchase, parts, and service invoices land on the asset without hand entry. Until a live integration exists, invoices arrive by hand and are marked MANUAL_ENTRY; PORTAL_SYNC is reserved for the live pull and nothing by hand may use it.

            
A pull always tells the truth
Every pull records its attempt on the link. With no live integration, the only truthful outcome is NOT_CONNECTED, and the attempt names its reason: a link with no portal address names that first; next, no login for the portal in the password vault; then no live integration. A pull never pretends invoices arrived.

            
Unlinking is refused while records ride on the link
A link with invoices or pull attempts on it cannot be unlinked — the refusal names how many of each ride on it, because those records point at the asset through the link. A link with nothing riding on it unlinks cleanly, and the asset is free to link again.

            
Invoice kinds, amounts, and duplicates
Every invoice on a link is one of PURCHASE, PARTS, or SERVICE. An amount of null means the amount is not on file — never zero — and it reads “Not on file.” The same portal invoice number twice on one link is a duplicate and is refused; the same number on a different link is a different invoice.

            
Who can do what
View: office titles (Owner, Operations Manager, Office Manager), the division managers (Construction, Maintenance), and the Shop/Fleet Manager. Write — link, unlink, pull, record invoices by hand: office titles plus the Shop/Fleet Manager; division managers read only. Crew titles and the CSR: no access at all.

Try adding a second link for an asset that already has one — refused. Add a link and leave the login step blank — refused; then tick no vendor site and it saves with the step marked “none.” Record an invoice by hand with the amount left blank — it lands as MANUAL_ENTRY with the amount Not on file, never $0. Then switch titles at the top: a division manager reads everything but every write is refused, and the CSR and crew titles get no access at all. Password Vault
One entry per site login — site name, site address, username, password, and a note. Lists show metadata only; a secret is served only to a vault-unlocked viewer whose title may see that entry.
Slice 95

          
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 95 — Password vaultThe vault opens with its own vault password, separate from the roster sign-in, and that password lives only in this page's memory while the vault is open — lock the vault or refresh and it is gone. Personal entries are visible only to the person who saved them; shared entries are visible by title — office titles see office portals, shop titles see parts portals, and the Owner sees all. Crew and CSR never see shared entries, and nobody sees another person's personal entries. Secrets are never stored in plain text and never shown in lists — reveal and fill serve the payload only to a vault-unlocked, authorized viewer. Every open, copy, or fill of a shared entry is logged, with who and when. A forgotten vault password means the Owner resets access and that person's personal entries must be re-entered. Passkeys are not built: entries carry no passkey, and fill falls back to the stored password. In this preview, two seeded vaults are already set up — Stephanie Valle's and Jake Lombard's — with the sample vault password ••••••••••••; everyone else sets their own. All entries, passwords, and log rows are samples.

          
Who sees whatLoading the vault for your title…

          


          
How the vault works
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 95

          

            
Its own password, held only in memory
The vault password is separate from the roster sign-in. It is checked against a scrambled record, never stored in plain text, and the unlocked state lives only in this page's memory while the vault is open. Locking the vault, switching the person at the top, or refreshing the page locks it again.

            
Personal is personal; shared goes by title
A personal entry is visible only to the person who saved it — not to the Owner, not to anyone else. A shared OFFICE entry is visible to the Owner, Operations Manager, Office Manager, Construction Manager, and Maintenance Manager. A shared SHOP entry is visible to the Owner, Operations Manager, Office Manager, and Shop/Fleet Manager. Crew and CSR never see shared entries. Shared entries are managed by the Owner, Operations Manager, and Office Manager, plus the owning division manager.

            
Every shared open, copy, and fill is logged
Opening, copying, or filling a shared entry writes a row to the shared access log with who did it and when. Personal entries are not logged — they are nobody else's business. The log shows each viewer only the scopes their title may see; the Owner sees the whole log.

            
Forgotten password: Owner reset, entries re-entered
There is no self-service recovery. When someone forgets their vault password, the Owner resets their access: the old vault password is cleared and that person's personal entries are wiped and must be re-entered. Shared entries are untouched — they belong to the company, not to one person's vault password.

            
Fill serves a payload — injection is not built
Fill serves the username and password payload that an app or browser extension would consume. Injecting that payload into a third-party login page is not built yet — nothing here types into another site's login form. Passkeys are not built: no entry carries a passkey, so fill falls back to the stored password.

            
The vendor-portal bridge
On a Vendor portals link (Slice 94), attaching a shared vault entry your title may see flips the link from PENDING_SETUP to LINKED; clearing it drops the link back. A personal entry can never back a link. The link's pull still reports NOT_CONNECTED and stays unverified — a login on file is not a live integration — but the pull reason now says honestly that a vault login is on file.

Open a shared entry — a row lands in the shared access log. Switch to the Shop/Fleet Manager (same sample password): the office portals disappear and the parts portals appear. Switch to a crew title: no shared entries at all, personal only. As the Owner, attach the shared Bobcat parts entry to the Bobcat link in Vendor portals — the link flips to LINKED, its pull still reads NOT_CONNECTED, and the reason now says a vault login is on file. Door Access
The shop's doors and the yard gate run as one access system — who can open what, when, and a log of every opening and every denied try.
Slice 83

          
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 83 — Door accessThe shop's doors plus the gate are ONE access system — the man door beside the gate is a door row of its own, linked to its gate. Every grant names exactly one of a person or a title — never both, never neither — and a door opens only when permission AND the time window both pass. Windows are read in America/New_York time — days of the week, start and end times, and dates — and a grant with no window is unrestricted. Every opening is logged (who, which door, when, with after-hours openings flagged) and denied attempts are logged too. The kill switch disables a roster account's app, door, and gate access together — office titles only — and queues a revocation per point; grants are never deleted by the kill switch. The gate takes tag/chip entry by a normalized opaque tag reference and exit by the inside loop, which is never denied. The video intercom is held as call records only (REQUESTED / ACTIVE / ENDED — no media), cameras are opaque stream references with views filtered by title, keypad entry is a PIN fallback with hashed PINs only (4–12 digits), and the controller snapshot carries the grants plus windows with its last pushed time. The people below are the real roster; door names, tag references, PIN hashes, events, and times are samples for this preview.

          
Who sees whatLoading door access for your title…

          


          
How door access works
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 83

          

            
One system — doors and the gate together
Doors and gates are access points in one system, under the same grants, the same windows, and the same log. The man door beside the gate is not part of the gate row — it is a door row of its own, linked to its gate, so a person can hold gate access without the man door, or the man door without the gate.

            
Exactly one — a person or a title
Every grant names one person or one title — never both, and never neither. A person grant follows that one person. A title grant follows whoever holds the title, so it reaches a new hire in that seat without a new grant — and it is also why the kill switch works on the account, not on the grant.

            
Permission AND window — both must pass
An opening is granted only when the person holds a grant for that point and the moment falls inside that grant's time window. Windows carry days of the week, a start and end time, and dates, all read in America/New_York local time. A grant with no window is unrestricted — it passes at any hour, on any day. Failing either leg is a denial, and the denial is logged with its reason.

            
Every opening logged — denials too
The log holds who, which door, and when for every opening, and an opening outside shop hours (before 6:00 AM, at or after 6:00 PM, or on a weekend) is flagged AFTER-HOURS. Denied attempts are logged the same way — no permission, outside the window, a disabled account, no PIN on file — each with the reason it failed.

            
The kill switch — app, door, and gate together
Disabling a roster account — office titles only: the Owner, the Operations Manager, the Office Manager — cuts that person's app sign-in, door access, and gate access in one move. A revocation is queued for each access point the person could open, and each one sits PENDING until a controller push carries it (pushes are not live — see the notice on this page). The person's grants are not deleted: they stay on the record, so re-enabling the account restores exactly the access that was there.

            
Gate — tag in, loop out
Gate entry is by tag/chip, recorded as a normalized opaque tag reference — the system stores the reference, never a readable credential number. Exit is by the inside loop: a vehicle crossing the loop on the way out opens the gate, and a loop exit is never denied — nobody is ever locked inside the yard.

            
Intercom — call records, no media
The video intercom is held as call records: each call is REQUESTED, then ACTIVE when answered, then ENDED — with who requested, who answered, and when. No audio or video is carried or stored on the record, and talking through the intercom is not live in this preview.

            
Cameras — references, filtered by title
Each camera is an opaque stream reference tied to the points it covers — no video plays here. Camera views are filtered by title: a title sees only the cameras it is cleared for, and in the door log each event names its covering camera only for titles cleared to view it — everyone else sees that the view is not available to their title.

            
Keypad PIN — hashed fallback only
The keypad is the fallback when a phone or tag is not at hand. A PIN is 4–12 digits and is stored hashed only — the plain PIN is never stored and never shown. Because live keypad reporting is not live, an opening made by PIN is recorded by an admin on this page and lands in the same door log, marked as admin-recorded.

            
Onboarding — complete is figured on read
Shop access is set up through a 7-item checklist per person: account created, app sign-in confirmed, grants set, window checked, gate tag issued, PIN set, and the access rules explained. Complete is computed on read — a person reads complete only while all 7 items stand done; nothing stores a "complete" flag.

            
Controller snapshot — pushes stay PENDING
The controllers at the doors run from a snapshot: the grants plus their windows. The snapshot shows its last pushed time; asking for a new push queues it as PENDING. In this preview a push never completes, because controller pushes are not live — the snapshot on this page is the record of what a push would carry.

          

          
Try itUse Try an opening: pick Danny Montes at the Parts room door on a weekday morning — he is denied, and the denial lands in the log, because no grant covers him there. Pick Michael Hehir at the Gate man door on a Saturday at 7:48 PM — the title grant's window runs to 8:00 PM, so it opens and is flagged AFTER-HOURS; try 9:30 PM and the same door is denied — outside the window. Set the method to Inside loop — exit at the gate: it opens for anyone, never denied. Then, as an office title, throw the kill switch on a roster account: app, door, and gate cut together, a PENDING revocation queues per point, and the person's grants stay on the record. Switch to a division manager title and the same switch is refused. Nothing in this preview is saved and nothing reaches a real door — decisions are logged here only, until the page is refreshed.

Bobcat portal
The Bobcat dealer portal, linked machine by machine to the CRM's own equipment. Links, parts-order drafts, and portal invoices recorded by hand — nothing here reaches the real portal.
Slice 86

          
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 86 — Bobcat portalOne portal machine id links once per connection, and one link per CRM asset — a second link for either is refused. A link stays UNVERIFIED until a live portal check confirms it, and unlinking is refused while orders or invoices ride on the link. Parts ordering is drafts only: a draft buys nothing, a person approves it, and an approved draft attaches to the CRM's own purchase order — it never becomes the purchase order. There is no sent-to-portal status: submitting is integration-gated and is never pretended. Quantities are whole numbers above zero; a unit price of null means not on file — never zero, and it shows as “Not on file.” Portal invoices are recorded by a person from what the portal shows — manual entry only; portal-sync is reserved for a future live integration, and a duplicate portal invoice for the same machine is refused. The connection carries NO credential, key, or secret anywhere — there is no field for one on this page. A live check honestly reports NOT_CONNECTED — no address on file, no credentials, no live verifier — and records the attempt; CONNECTED is reachable only through a future live verification, never by writing a status. Setup records PENDING_SETUP progress only. The machines below are real units from the Equipment list; every portal machine id, part number, price, and invoice number on this page is a sample. Viewing is office titles plus division managers; writes are office titles plus the Shop/Fleet Manager. Crew and CSR never get access.

          
Who sees whatLoading the Bobcat portal for your title…

          


          
How the Bobcat portal works
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 86

          

            
One link per machine id, one link per asset
On this connection, a portal machine id can be linked once — linking the same id again, to any asset, is refused. And a CRM asset carries one link — linking a second portal id to an asset that already has one is refused. The link is the one bridge between what the portal calls the machine and what the CRM calls the asset.

            
Unverified until a live check confirms it
Every new link is born UNVERIFIED. It becomes verified only when a live portal check actually reaches the portal and confirms that machine id — never because a person typed a status, and never because the link was created carefully. In this preview no live check can pass, so every link here reads UNVERIFIED, honestly.

            
Unlinking is refused while work rides on the link
A link with parts drafts or portal invoices on it cannot be unlinked — the refusal names how many of each ride on it. Those records point at the machine through the link; cutting the link would strand them. A link with nothing riding on it unlinks cleanly, and its portal id and asset are free to link again.

            
Drafts only — a draft buys nothing
Parts ordering here never orders. A draft is a list a person is preparing: it buys nothing, reserves nothing, and sends nothing. A draft becomes useful only when a person approves it — approval is a person's act, recorded with their name, never automatic.

            
An approved draft attaches to the CRM's own PO
An approved draft is attached to a purchase order the CRM already holds — picked from the CRM's own PO list. The draft never becomes the purchase order: the PO stays the CRM's record, and the draft rides on it as the parts list behind it. An unapproved draft cannot be attached.

            
No sent-to-portal status — ever
There is no “sent to portal” status on a draft, and nothing on this page pretends to submit one. Submitting to the portal is integration-gated: until a live integration exists, the Submit action refuses and says why, and the draft's status does not move. Draft statuses are only DRAFT and APPROVED.

            
Quantities and prices — whole numbers, null is not zero
A quantity is a whole number above zero — zero, a negative, or a fraction like 1.5 is refused. A unit price can be null, which means not on file — the price simply isn't known yet. Null is never shown as $0.00 and never stored as zero: a zero price would claim the part is free, and null claims nothing. Leave the price blank on the form and the line records Not on file.

            
Portal invoices — recorded by a person, by hand
A portal invoice enters the CRM only when a person records it from what the portal shows — its number, date, and total, typed in. Manual entry is the only way in. Portal-sync is reserved for a future live integration: the Sync action refuses today and imports nothing. And a duplicate is refused: the same portal invoice number recorded twice for the same machine is stopped — the same number on a different machine is a different invoice and is allowed.

            
No credential, key, or secret — anywhere
The connection record holds no credential, no API key, no password, no secret — there is no field for one on the connection, on a link, on a draft, or on an invoice, and nothing on this page asks for one. When a live integration is built, how it authenticates is that integration's design — it is not pre-stored here.

            
The live check tells the truth: NOT_CONNECTED
Running a live check today reports NOT_CONNECTED, with the three reasons stated plainly: no portal address on file for the connection, no credentials held (by design — see above), and no live verifier available to this preview. The check records the attempt — who ran it and when — in the check history. CONNECTED can only ever be the result of a future live verification; it is never a status a person can pick or write.

            
Setup — PENDING_SETUP progress only
Connection setup records progress, and its standing status is PENDING_SETUP — steps done are noted, by whom, and the status does not advance to connected or complete from anything recorded here. Setup finishes only when a future live verification passes, which is the same gate as CONNECTED.

            
Who sees it, who writes it
Viewing: the Owner, the Operations Manager, the Office Manager, and the division managers — Construction, Maintenance, and Shop/Fleet. Writes — linking, unlinking, drafts, approvals, attaching to a PO, recording invoices, running checks, recording setup progress — belong to the office titles plus the Shop/Fleet Manager; the Construction and Maintenance managers read only. Crew titles and the CSR get no access at all — the menu entry is hidden for them.

          

          
Try itAs the Owner, tap Run live check: it reports NOT_CONNECTED — no address on file, no credentials, no live verifier — and the attempt lands in the check history. Try to link portal id BC-E55-011531 again and it is refused — already linked once; try any new id on the Bobcat E55 and it is refused — one link per asset. Try to unlink the E55 and it is refused because a portal invoice rides on it; unlink the skid steer after its draft is dealt with and it goes through. On the skid-steer draft, read the filter line: its price is Not on file — null, never $0.00. Tap Submit to portal on any draft: it refuses, integration-gated, and no sent status appears. Approve the draft, then attach it to PO-1086 — the draft rides on the CRM's own PO and stays a draft record. Record the E55's invoice number again on the E55 — refused as a duplicate; record it on another machine and it is allowed. Tap Sync from portal — refused; sync is reserved. Then switch titles at the top: a division manager reads everything but every write is refused, the Shop/Fleet Manager can write, and the CSR and crew titles get no access. Nothing in this preview is saved, and nothing reaches the real Bobcat portal — records last until the page is refreshed.

        


        

          
Fuel
The fuel hub: authorize at the pump, watch the four tank ledgers, reconcile, and link off-site purchases — all on one record layer.
Slices 60 + 64

          
Slices 60 + 64 — Fuel records, fuel screens, and the pump terminalThere is no employee fuel PIN anywhere in this system — not at the pump, not at the terminal, not on this page. The signed-in app session is the identity. The camera at the pump checks the face against that session: a match authorizes, a mismatch is a hard deny, and a no-result — the camera can't read a face — needs a manager's approval in the app. Every attempt, authorized or not, writes a fuel event. All names, gallons, and amounts below are sample samples.

Pump authorization — Slice 64
This is the screen the pump shows. You are already signed in — that session is who you are. There is nothing to type: no PIN, no fuel credential. Try the three camera outcomes.
Pump 1 · Shop yard

          

            

              
Signed in as (app session = identity)Danny Montes · Crew A

              
Fuel credential / PINNone — never asked, nowhere in the system

              

                

                

              

              
Camera face check — simulate the outcome:

              

                
                
                
              

              
Waiting for the camera checkPick an outcome above. A match authorizes the pump. A no-result holds for a manager. A mismatch denies — full stop.

              

            

            

              
The authorization rules — the same everywhere

              
    
                
  • Face match → authorized. The fuel event is written under the signed-in employee, the product, and the vehicle.
    • 
                
  • Camera no-result → hold. No fuel moves until a manager approves it in the app. The approval is recorded on the event, with the manager's name.
    • 
                
  • Face mismatch → hard deny. Not a hold, not an override. A manager approval attached to a mismatch changes nothing — the event is recorded as denied and the pump stays locked.
    • 
                
  • Terminal seam: the pump reader at the terminal talks to the CRM through the same authorization service — same session identity, same camera rules, same event record. A mismatch at the terminal is a hard deny there too, even with a manager approval attached.
    •

What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 90 — Visual polygon editorPick a fence below and it is drawn on the map as a polygon, with the place's site pin and its numbered corners marked on it. Reshape the polygon in the vertex table under the map — it edits latitude and longitude directly and deletes vertices, and Add vertex places a new vertex on the longest edge — but a fence never drops below 3 vertices. Save shape saves the redraw and confirms the fence in the same step; Confirm as-is confirms the fence without changing its vertices. The map frames the fence when you pick it. Slice 90

            

          

          
How geofences work
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 90

          

            
Save shape saves and confirms together
Save shape is one step, not two: the redrawn vertices are saved and the fence reads CONFIRMED from that moment — the person who redrew it is the person who confirmed it. Confirm as-is is the other path: it confirms the fence exactly as it stands, without changing a single vertex — any unsaved redraw on screen is put back, and the record says the shape was confirmed as it was.

            
A shape that crosses itself is refused
If the redrawn polygon's edges cross each other, Save shape is refused and the refusal names the error: SELF_INTERSECTING_POLYGON. Nothing is saved and the fence keeps its last saved shape and its old status. Fix the crossing corners — move them apart in the table or delete one — and save again.

            
A pin outside its polygon only warns
The site pin is where the place itself sits; the polygon is the ground the crew has to be on. When the pin falls outside the polygon, the editor shows a warning — and that is all it does. Saving and confirming still go through. The warning stays on the fence until the shape or the pin is fixed, so nobody mistakes silence for a check that passed.

            
Three vertices, minimum — and fit once per pick
A polygon needs at least 3 vertices: the table's delete button stops at three, and a save below three is refused. The map frames the fence when the fence is picked, and the Fit to fence button frames it again whenever you tap it.

            
A new fence starts UNCONFIRMED
Creating a fence takes a kind, a reference id, a name, and the site pin's latitude and longitude — all four, or the create is refused and names what is missing. Your own vertices are optional: leave them out and the system suggests a polygon around the pin for a person to reshape. Either way the new fence starts UNCONFIRMED — a person still has to look at it and save or confirm it. A second fence with the same kind and reference id is refused: one fence per place.

            
Owner and Operations Manager write; everyone else views
Only the Owner and the Operations Manager can add or delete corners, save, confirm, or create a fence. The Office Manager, the division managers, and the Shop/Fleet Manager open the page and see every fence, its shape, and its status — view only, with the editing controls held off. Crew and CSR titles do not get the page at all.

          

          
Try Slice 90Open the David Gable fence: its site pin sits outside its polygon, so the editor warns — then Save shape anyway and watch it save, warning and all. Now move one corner of the Center 111 fence in the vertex table across the opposite edge so the shape bows into a bowtie, and Save shape — it is refused as SELF_INTERSECTING_POLYGON. Put the corner back and use Confirm as-is instead: the fence reads CONFIRMED and not one vertex moved. Switch to the Office Manager role (tap your title, top right) and the same page is view-only. Back as Owner, create a fence with kind JOBSITE and reference id WO-SAMPLE-1042 — it is refused as a duplicate of the Claris fence.

Setup
The one-time company setup: eight sections, each figured live from this preview's own records — the company profile, the rate records, the budget rows, and the files put on record through the upload intake below. Nothing here is auto-filled, and nothing is guessed.
Slice 85

          
What's new — Nov 3, 2026 · Slice 85 — Setup prompt + document/list uploadsSetup runs once. An office title — the Owner, the Operations Manager, or the Office Manager — starts it; starting it a second time, or starting it after it is completed, is refused. The eight sections below are computed live from the records this preview already holds: company identity and registrations read the company profile and the licenses library; tax rates and workers' comp rates read the burden-rate records on Cost Tracking; overhead reads the current-year overhead budget row — no row means the section reads visibly unset, never a guessed figure, and setting it takes both a total and a rate, each entered explicitly, never a default rate; wage bands, vendor lists, and setup documents read what has been filed through the upload intake. Completing setup is Owner only, and completing records an attestation that names the sections still unanswered at that moment — completion is not a forcing gate: setup can be completed with sections still open, and the attestation says so plainly. Uploads take PDF, CSV, text, and image files only, from 1 byte to 10 MB, and every upload is given a server-generated storage key, shown on its row. Lists must be CSV and are parsed at intake; their rows are stored as raw strings — a price of “12.50” stays the string “12.50”, never a number. Each kind proposes a filing target — a document proposes the company profile, vendor prices propose the vendor list, wage bands propose wage bands, and Other proposes NONE: a NONE row forces an explicit choice and is never default-filed to the profile. A row that cannot be filed goes to the exceptions queue with its reason, stays listed, and can still be filed later by a person; an unparseable CSV lands there too, with its parse reason — never dropped. Filing a list puts the list on file only — it creates no vendor, price, or wage-band records. No password, key, or secret column exists on any setup record, and a credential column inside an upload is dropped at intake, never stored. Company-knowledge upload — SOPs and HR documents — is not part of this and is not built here.

          
Who sees whatLoading setup for your title…

          


          
How setup works
The rules behind this page, in plain words.
Slice 85

          

            
Eight sections — figured live, nothing auto-filled
Each section's state is figured from the records at the moment the page is read — the company profile, the licenses & COI library, the burden-rate records, the overhead budget row, and the filed uploads. Nothing is ever auto-filled: a value appears only because a record holds it or a person entered it. A section with nothing behind it reads Unanswered, in plain sight.

            
Overhead — both a total and a rate, or it stays unset
The overhead section reads the current-year (2026) overhead budget row. While no row stands, the section reads UNSET — it never borrows the division-budget total, never carries a figure over from another panel, and never shows a guessed number. Creating the row takes both a total and a rate, each typed in explicitly: the rate box starts empty, because there is no default rate to lean on. One without the other is refused.

            
Start once — a second start is refused
Setup is started once, by an office title. Tapping Start again while setup is under way is refused, and starting after setup has been completed is refused too — a completed setup is not reopened by starting over. The record keeps who started it and when.

            
Completion — Owner only, with an attestation
Only the Owner can complete setup. Completing writes an attestation: who completed it, when, how many of the eight sections stood answered, and the names of the sections still unanswered at that moment. It is not a forcing gate — the Owner may complete with sections still open, and the attestation records exactly that, so the gap is on the record instead of hidden.

            
Uploads — accepted files, generated keys
The intake accepts PDF, CSV, text, and image files only, sized 1 byte to 10 MB. Every accepted upload is given a storage key generated for it — the uploader never names the storage location — and the key is shown on the upload's row from intake onward, including after it is filed.

            
Lists — CSV only, parsed at intake, rows stay raw strings
A list upload must be a CSV. It is parsed when it arrives: the header and every row are read then, not later. The rows are stored as raw strings — exactly the characters in the file. A price written “12.50” is stored as the string “12.50” with its trailing zero; it is never turned into a number, so nothing is rounded, trimmed, or reformatted on the way in.

            
Proposed targets — and NONE means choose
Each kind proposes where its upload files: Document → Company profile, Vendor prices → Vendor list, Wage bands → Wage bands, Other → NONE. A proposal can be changed before confirming — except that NONE is not a destination: an Other upload sits unfiled until a person explicitly chooses its target. It is never default-filed to the company profile just to clear the row.

            
Exceptions — listed with a reason, fileable later
A row that cannot be filed — no target chosen, or a CSV that could not be parsed — goes to the exceptions queue with the reason written on it. It stays listed; nothing in the queue is silently dropped. A person can still file an exception row later by choosing its target on the queue row itself — the parse reason stays on the record, so the file's history is honest.

            
Filing a list creates nothing but the filing
Confirming a vendor price list files the list — it creates no vendor records and no price records. Confirming a wage-band list creates no wage-band records. The sections above count filed lists, and the Vendors page and the rate records are exactly as they were before the filing.

            
No secrets on any setup record
No password, key, or secret column exists on the setup record, on an upload row, or on a filed list — there is nowhere on this page that holds a credential. If an uploaded CSV carries a credential column (a password, an API key, a token), that column is dropped at intake and never stored; the row notes how many columns were dropped, and the rest of the list is kept.

            
Not part of setup — company knowledge
Company-knowledge upload is not built here. SOPs and HR documents do not come in through this intake; the Help Desk library is their home. This intake is for setup documents and setup lists only — the company profile's paperwork, vendor price lists, and wage-band lists.

            
Office titles only
Setup is open to the Owner, the Operations Manager, and the Office Manager — and to no other title. Those three can start setup and work the intake; completion is the Owner alone. Every other title gets no access — the menu entry is hidden for them, and setup itself is not shown to them here either.

          

          
Try itAs an office title, tap Start setup — then tap it again and the second start is refused. Read the eight sections: identity, registrations, tax rates, and comp rates stand answered from the records already on file, while wage bands, overhead, vendor lists, and setup documents read unanswered — overhead UNSET, with no figure shown for it anywhere. In the intake, add the sample vendor price list: it parses at intake, its prices show in quotes as raw strings (“12.50” keeps its zero), and confirming files it to the vendor list — the Vendor lists section flips to answered, and the Vendors page gains no new vendor. Add the sample Other upload and try to confirm it with no target chosen — it lands in the exceptions queue; choose a target there and file it from the queue. Add the broken CSV — it goes to exceptions with its parse reason. Add the list with a password column — the credential columns are dropped before anything is stored. Set the overhead row with only a total — refused; add the rate and it stands. Then switch to the Owner and complete setup: the attestation names the sections still unanswered, and Start is refused from then on. Nothing in this preview is saved — setup and its uploads last until the page is refreshed.

Qualification script
The questions to ask on a first call or text back — the same questions behind each lead's 🎯 Perfect Client fit score. Ask them in order, write the answers on the lead, and blanks never punish: only answered questions count toward the score.

      

        
Open

        
“Thanks for reaching out to Gold Coast Property Maintenance — let me ask a few quick questions so the right person calls you back with the right next step.”

        
    
          
  1. What work are you looking to have done, and at what property? (Get the street address and town.)
    2. 
          
  2. Is this your property — and are you the person who decides on this work?
    3. 
          
  3. What is the best phone number and email to reach you?
    4. 
        

        
Construction — ask

        
    
          
  • What is the budget for this project?
    • 
          
  • Does the contact own the property?
    • 
          
  • Is the budget approved / funded and ready to go?
    • 
          
  • Is the contact the person who decides on this work?
    • 
          
  • Is the property within our service area?
    • 
          
  • Is the timeline flexible (no hard deadline)?
    • 
        

        
Maintenance — ask

        
    
          
  • Will this be recurring weekly service (not a one-time job)?
    • 
          
  • What is the property size?
    • 
          
  • Is the contact the decision maker (homeowner or HOA contact who can say yes)?
    • 
          
  • Is the property within 20 miles of the Monroe shop?
    • 
          
  • Will they keep a payment method on file and agree to standard terms?
    • 
          
  • Do they want full-service care (mowing + treatments + cleanups), not mow-only?
    • 
        

        
Snow — ask

        
    
          
  • Is this a commercial property or HOA (not a single driveway)?
    • 
          
  • Will they sign a seasonal contract (not per-storm only)?
    • 
          
  • Is the decision maker reachable before storms?
    • 
          
  • Is the property within our snow service area?
    • 
          
  • Do they have multiple properties we could service?
    • 
        

        
Close

        
“The next step is a site walk so we can price it exactly. I'll put you in the pipeline now and [the division manager] will call you back to set it up.”
